14050:
When you describe someone or something as spruce, you mean they look neat, clean, and smartly put-together. It's the kind of neatness that suggests effort and care — not just "not messy," but actively well-presented and trim in appearance.

Think of a man who has ironed his shirt perfectly, combed his hair carefully, and polished his shoes. He looks spruce. Or imagine a small house with a freshly painted door, trimmed hedges, and clean windows. That house looks spruce too.

The word does more than just say "neat." It carries a specific flavour:

  • It suggests deliberate effort — someone or something didn't accidentally look this way. There was care involved.
  • It implies a pleasant, satisfying tidiness — not cold or sterile, but crisp and pleasing to the eye.
  • It often hints at a smart, almost stylish quality — not necessarily fashionable, but proper and well-kept.

So while "clean" simply means dirt-free, and "tidy" means things are in order, spruce combines both and adds that extra layer of sharp, well-groomed smartness.

The adjective can be used for:

People — their overall appearance, clothes, or grooming:

"He looked very spruce in his freshly pressed uniform."
"She arrived at the interview looking spruce and confident."

Places — homes, rooms, gardens, offices:

"The little cottage looked surprisingly spruce after the renovation."
"The office was spruce and orderly, everything in its right place."

Objects — anything that has been kept in sharp, clean condition:

"His car, though old, was always kept spruce."

When you call someone or something spruce, you are almost always giving a compliment. It communicates:

  • "You've made an effort."
  • "You care about how you present yourself (or your space)."
  • "You look sharp and respectable."

It's a warm word. It doesn't imply someone is overdressed or trying too hard — it simply means they look just right: clean, crisp, and properly put-together.

Spruce sits at a moderate level of neatness and smartness — not casual, but not extravagant either. Here's a rough sense of scale:

  • Sloppy / scruffy → messy and careless
  • Decent / presentable → acceptable, but no real effort
  • Spruce → neat, trim, smartly turned out ✓
  • Immaculate / impeccable → absolutely flawless, almost perfect
  • Overdressed / flashy → too much effort, too showy

Spruce is the sweet spot of everyday, admirable neatness.

Understanding how spruce compares to similar words will sharpen your grasp of it:

  • Neat — the most general word for tidy and orderly. Spruce is more specific and more complimentary than neat.
  • Trim — suggests a clean, precise, lean quality. Spruce includes trim-ness but adds a warmer, more personal sense of grooming.
  • Dapper — almost always used for men and focuses heavily on stylish, well-chosen clothing. Spruce is broader — it applies to people of any gender, and to places and things too. Also, dapper leans more towards style; spruce leans more towards clean neatness.
  • Smart (British English) — in the British sense of well-dressed, "smart" is very close to spruce, but smart can also refer to intelligence. Spruce is unambiguously about appearance.
  • Well-groomed — focuses on personal hygiene and grooming (hair, skin, nails). Spruce includes this but is wider — it covers clothing, surroundings, and overall presentation.

To fully own a word, know its opposites:

  • Scruffy — untidy, rough, and uncared-for in appearance
  • Unkempt — untidy, especially of hair or clothing, as if no attention has been paid
  • Dishevelled — messy and disarranged, often after some kind of activity
  • Slovenly — habitually messy and careless about appearance
  • Shabby — worn-out and neglected-looking

This is important to know because you will encounter it often. "To spruce up" means to make someone or something look neater, cleaner, and more attractive — to improve the appearance through tidying or grooming.

"She spruced up the living room before the guests arrived." (tidied and freshened it)
"He spruced himself up before the job interview." (groomed himself carefully)
"The old building was spruced up with a coat of paint." (made to look smart again)

The verb phrase carries the same core idea as the adjective — the end result of "sprucing up" something is that it looks spruce.

• Spruce is a slightly formal or literary word. You'll see it in writing and hear it from older or more careful speakers. It's not archaic — it's still in active use — but it's less common in very casual, everyday speech.
  • It is more common in British English than American English, though it is understood and used in both.
  • It is almost always used positively. You would rarely use spruce sarcastically.

Spruce (adjective): Looking neat, clean, trim, and smartly presented — in a way that shows deliberate care and effort. It applies to people, places, and things, and always carries a positive, complimentary tone.

If you remember one image: picture a well-pressed, clean outfit on a person standing tall — not flashy, not sloppy, just perfectly put-together. That is spruce.
14051: To spruce up means to make something or someone look noticeably cleaner, neater, fresher, or more attractive — usually through small, careful improvements. Think of it as giving something a light "refresh" — not a dramatic transformation, just a positive, noticeable polish.

The verb "spruce" is almost never used alone. It is nearly always paired with the word "up," forming the phrasal verb "spruce up."

You will almost never hear: "I spruced the room."
You will almost always hear: "I spruced up the room."

So whenever you see or use this word as a verb, think of it as spruce up — the two words work together as a unit.

Three broad categories of things get spruced up:

1. Places
Rooms, houses, offices, gardens, shops, parks, entire neighbourhoods or cities.

2. Things
Cars, furniture, websites, documents, presentations, outfits.

3. People (including yourself)
Appearance, grooming, clothing — how a person looks overall.

• "She spruced up the apartment before her parents arrived."

She cleaned, tidied, and perhaps added some fresh flowers or decorative touches to make it look welcoming and presentable.

  • "He spruced himself up before the job interview."

He showered, fixed his hair, ironed his clothes — generally made himself look neat and sharp.

  • "The city spruced up the old park with new benches and a fresh coat of paint."

Small, visible improvements were made to make the park look more pleasant.

  • "Let's spruce up this presentation before we send it to the client."

Let's polish it — maybe improve the layout, clean up the fonts, make it look more professional.

  • "The café was spruced up with bright new walls and better lighting."

The café was given a light makeover to look more attractive and inviting.

This is what makes "spruce up" a precise word. It always implies moderate, cosmetic-level improvement — not a major overhaul.

Think of it on a spectrum:

Light touch → Spruce up → Major renovation → Complete transformation

  • Painting a wall = sprucing up. Knocking it down and rebuilding = not sprucing up.
  • Combing your hair and putting on a nice shirt = sprucing up. Buying an entirely new wardrobe = not sprucing up.
  • Refreshing a few sections of a website = sprucing up. Rebuilding it from scratch = not sprucing up.

If the changes are massive, people use stronger words like renovate, overhaul, revamp, or transform. "Spruce up" is reserved specifically for lighter, visible, positive improvements.

"Spruce up" is informal and conversational. It carries a warm, cheerful, upbeat quality. It's the kind of phrase you'd use when chatting with a friend, not in a formal business report or legal document. And the feeling around it is always positive — sprucing something up is always seen as a good, helpful thing to do.

Pattern 1 — With a place or thing:

Spruce up + [the thing]
"We spruced up the office."
"They are sprucing up the town square."

Pattern 2 — With a person or reflexively (about yourself):

Spruce up + [the person] / Spruce + yourself + up
"Go spruce yourself up before dinner."
"I need to spruce myself up a bit."
"The stylist spruced him up for the photoshoot."

Note that when used reflexively, you can also simply say "go spruce up" when the meaning is clear from context — "You have five minutes to spruce up before we leave."
To spruce up means to make something or someone look fresher, neater, or more attractive through light, careful improvements — not a dramatic transformation, just a noticeable, positive polish.
14052:
Spry means active, lively, and energetic in a light, quick, and effortless way — particularly when this energy is surprising given a person's age or physical condition.

Think of it this way: when most people grow old, they slow down, move carefully, and tire easily. But occasionally, you meet an 80-year-old who walks briskly, thinks sharply, laughs easily, and moves around with the kind of ease you'd expect from someone much younger. That person is spry.

The word is almost always used as a quiet compliment that carries an unspoken "for their age" inside it. When you call someone spry, you are essentially saying: "They are far more energetic and lively than I would have expected."

Spry can describe both the body and the mind, and often both at once.

Physical spryness means moving with quickness, lightness, and agility — getting up without struggle, walking without hesitation, or carrying out physical tasks with surprising ease.

"At 85, my grandfather is still spry enough to tend his garden every morning."

Mental spryness means being sharp, alert, and quick-thinking — following conversations easily, recalling things quickly, and engaging with the world with a clear, active mind.

"She's 91 years old, but mentally she's incredibly spry — she reads two books a week."

Most of the time, calling someone spry implies both — a general vitality that shows in how they move and how they think.
The Key Nuance: Who Is Called Spry?

This is very important for using the word correctly.

Spry is almost always used for older people. You would almost never call a healthy 25-year-old "spry." That would sound strange, or even slightly sarcastic. The word gets its meaning and its power from the contrast — the contrast between the physical decline that old age typically brings, and the surprising energy this particular person still has.

So, the word quietly contains a comparison inside it:

  • Not just "this person is energetic."
  • But rather: "This person is energetic in spite of what age or hardship usually does to people."

This is why spry always carries a tone of admiration and pleasant surprise.
The Feeling the Word Carries (Tone and Connotation)

Spry is always a positive, warm, and admiring word. It is never insulting. When you call someone spry, you are genuinely impressed by them.

It also has a slightly informal, conversational feel — it's the kind of word you'd say to a friend, not write in a legal document. It feels friendly and natural in everyday speech.
How Spry Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close to spry, but none are quite the same.

  • Agile simply means able to move quickly and easily. It doesn't carry the "surprising for one's age" meaning.
  • Nimble means quick and light in movement or thought, but again, doesn't imply age.
  • Energetic just means having a lot of energy — very broad and neutral.
  • Sprightly is perhaps the closest synonym to spry. It means lively and cheerful in movement. The two words are nearly interchangeable, but spry more strongly emphasizes the contrast with expected age-related decline.

What makes spry unique is that single, powerful implication: "more lively than their years would suggest." None of its near-synonyms carry that implication as naturally or as strongly.

If spry describes surprising energy and liveliness in old age, the opposite ideas are captured by words like frail, feeble, sluggish, lethargic, or slow. These describe what spry is the happy exception to.

In real life, you'll often hear spry used with these kinds of phrases:

  • "Still spry" — the most common pattern. "She's 78 and still spry." The word "still" reinforces the idea of defying time.
  • "Surprisingly spry" or "remarkably spry" — emphasizing the pleasant shock of it.
  • "Spry old man/woman" — a classic combination.

1. "The spry 90-year-old beat everyone at chess without breaking a sweat."
  2. "Don't underestimate him — he may have white hair, but he's as spry as someone half his age."
  3. "After her hip surgery, the doctors were amazed at how spry she became again."
  4. "The old dog chased the ball with a spry energy that made everyone laugh." (Yes — spry can also describe animals.)

If you had to carry just one idea with you, it's this:

Spry means lively, quick, and energetic in a way that is pleasantly surprising — especially for someone who is old.
14053:
Spume is the white, bubbly, frothy foam that forms on the surface of water — especially the sea — when it is violently disturbed or agitated. Think of the moment a wave crashes hard against a rocky shore and explodes into a mass of white, fizzing, airy bubbles. That white, bubbly mass clinging to the rocks, swirling in the water, or being carried by the wind? That is spume.

It is essentially what happens when water gets so violently churned up that it traps air inside itself and turns into a light, fizzy, foamy substance.

Spume is white or off-white. It is light and airy. It is made of countless tiny bubbles packed so closely together that the whole thing looks like a thick, wet foam. It can sit on the surface of the water, cling to rocks and sand, or — when the wind is strong — get picked up and carried through the air in small, drifting, wispy clumps. It disappears quickly. It is fleeting. It forms, it drifts, it pops, and it is gone.

When a body of water — most commonly the sea — is disturbed with great force, the motion violently mixes air into the water. This trapped air forms bubbles. When billions of these bubbles cluster together on the surface, the result is spume. The stronger the disturbance — a crashing wave, a powerful storm, a churning current — the more spume is produced. This is why you see the most spume during rough weather or where waves crash hardest.

Spume is overwhelmingly associated with the sea, and that is its most natural home. You will encounter it:

  • On the crests of waves during a storm, where the wind blows it off the top of the waves into the air.
  • Where waves smash against rocks, cliffs, or a harbour wall, shattering into a mass of white froth.
  • Along the tideline on a beach after a rough sea, where it gathers in clumps and gets blown along the sand.
  • In rivers or waterfalls where water crashes powerfully over rocks and churns into foam.

While spume is most strongly tied to the sea, the word can technically be used for any similar frothy substance on any turbulent liquid.
Spume vs. Foam vs. Froth — What Is the Difference?

These three words are close relatives, and it is worth understanding how spume stands apart.

Foam is the broad, general, everyday word for any mass of bubbles on a liquid. You can have foam on your coffee, on soapy washing-up water, on a glass of beer, or on the sea. It is neutral and universal.

Froth is very similar to foam — light, airy bubbles — but it often suggests something even lighter and more delicate. You froth milk for a cappuccino. Beer has froth on top. Like foam, it works in many everyday contexts.

Spume is different in feel and in use. Here is what sets it apart:

First, spume is specifically and strongly associated with the sea and wild, turbulent water. While foam and froth feel comfortable in a kitchen or café, spume feels out of place there. Spume belongs to crashing waves, stormy shores, and powerful currents. It carries the energy and wildness of the ocean with it.

Second, spume implies force and violence of movement. It is not gentle bubbles. It is foam produced by something dramatic — a wave breaking with power, a sea churned by a gale. The word itself carries a sense of energy and turbulence.

Third, spume is a literary and poetic word. It is not the word you would use in casual everyday conversation. People do not say "I spilled my coffee and it made spume." But a novelist writing about a storm at sea, or a poet describing the ocean, would reach for the word "spume" because it is vivid, precise, and evocative in a way that plain "foam" is not. It paints a more dramatic, powerful picture.
The Feel and Tone of the Word

Spume is a word with weight and atmosphere. When a writer uses it, they are not just describing foam — they are evoking a scene of wild, dramatic, elemental nature. It sounds raw. It sounds powerful. It fits perfectly in writing about the sea in a storm, a ship being battered by waves, or a desolate, windswept coastline.

If you read the word "spume" in a book or a poem, you can be confident the author is deliberately choosing it over "foam" to make the scene feel more vivid, more wild, and more forceful.

Here are several example sentences that show how the word is used, from simple to more literary:

  • The storm churned the sea into great masses of spume.
  • Spume flew from the tops of the waves and stung her face.
  • He watched the spume gather in white clumps along the base of the cliff.
  • The ship ploughed through dark water, its bow sending white spume high into the air on either side.
  • After the storm, the beach was littered with clumps of pale spume that the wind shifted slowly across the sand.
The One Thing to Hold Onto

If you want to anchor this word in your memory with a single, clean idea, hold onto this:

Spume is the wild, white, frothy foam of the sea — born from force, carried by the wind, and gone in moments.

It is foam, but foam with drama. Foam with salt and wind and crashing waves behind it. That is spume.
14054: At the heart of every meaning of "spur" is a single picture: something sharp or pointed that either sticks out or pushes something forward. Hold onto that image. It will make every meaning feel logical rather than something you have to memorize.
The original, literal meaning — the device on a rider's boot

A spur is a small, sharp device that a horse rider straps to the heel of their boot. When the rider presses their heel into the horse's side, the spur digs in, giving the horse a signal to move faster or change direction. Some spurs are a simple pointed spike; others have a small spinning wheel with teeth at the end (called a rowel). Either way, the job is to give the horse a nudge — or a firm push.

This is the root from which almost every other meaning of "spur" branches out.

You may have heard the phrase "earning your spurs." Historically, a young knight was awarded his spurs when he proved himself in battle — they were the symbol of achievement and honor. Today, we still say someone has "earned their spurs" when they have proven their worth through hard work or a difficult challenge.
The figurative meaning — a motivation or stimulus

Because a spur literally pushes a horse into action, the word naturally came to mean anything that pushes a person (or a process) forward. In this sense, a spur is a motivation, an incentive, or a trigger — something that causes action.

  • "The threat of failure was the spur she needed to start studying."
  • "Competition can be a powerful spur to innovation."
  • "His coach's harsh words acted as a spur rather than a discouragement."

There is no physical object in these sentences. The spur is a force — a circumstance or feeling that jolts someone into moving. This is the most common way the word appears in everyday modern language.
The most essential phrase: "on the spur of the moment"

This is a phrase you will encounter constantly in English, and you must know it well.

"On the spur of the moment" means doing something impulsively — suddenly, without planning or thinking it through beforehand. The image is of a rider spontaneously digging their spurs in and charging forward without deliberation.

  • "On the spur of the moment, he quit his job and moved to another city."
  • "She bought the dress on the spur of the moment and later wasn't sure about it."
  • "It was a spur-of-the-moment trip — we just packed bags and left."

Notice "spur-of-the-moment" is also used as a compound adjective before a noun (a spur-of-the-moment decision). Whenever something is spontaneous, unplanned, and driven by impulse, this phrase fits perfectly.
The sharp projection on a bird's leg

Some birds — most famously roosters (male chickens) and certain game birds — have a hard, sharp, bony point growing naturally from the back of their leg. This too is called a spur. It is essentially a natural weapon the bird uses to slash and fight rivals. A rooster's spur can be quite long and dangerously sharp.

In botany, a spur is a slender, hollow, tube-like extension that sticks out from a petal or sepal of certain flowers. It usually holds nectar inside and points backward from the main part of the flower, attracting insects and birds to reach in for the nectar — which in turn helps pollination.

Flowers like columbine, violet, and larkspur have spurs. You may already know the word larkspur — a common garden flower whose very name contains the word, because its petal has a distinctive spur-shaped projection.
The ridge of land jutting from a hill or mountain

In geography, a spur is a narrow, finger-like ridge of higher land that projects outward from a main mountain or hill range. Picture the mountain range as a body and the spurs as arms or fingers stretching outward from it into the lower land around it.

Spurs are important to hikers and navigators. On a topographic map, a spur appears as a tongue of high land poking into surrounding lower terrain. Being able to identify them helps a hiker understand the shape of the land they're walking through.
The branch road or railway line

A spur (or "spur line" or "spur road") is a short road or railway track that branches off from a main route and leads to a specific location — often a town, factory, or terminal — without connecting through to anywhere else. It is essentially a dead-end branch.

Think of the main railway line as a tree trunk, and the spur as a short branch shooting off to one side, ending at a specific destination.

  • "The industrial site was connected to the rail network by a short spur."
  • "They built a spur road off the highway to serve the new development."

Look at every meaning side by side:

  • A boot spur → a sharp point that sticks out and pushes the horse forward
  • A motivational spur → something that pushes a person forward
  • "On the spur of the moment" → acting suddenly and impulsively, as if spurred
  • A bird's spur → a sharp point that juts out from the leg
  • A flower's spur → a projection that juts out from the petal
  • A geographical spur → a ridge that juts out from a mountain
  • A road or railway spur → a line that branches out from the main route

Every single one comes back to the same core: a pointed thing that sticks out, or something that drives forward. You don't need to memorize these meanings as separate, unrelated facts — they are all the same word, doing the same job in different contexts.
14055:
To spur something or someone means to cause, encourage, or push something to happen — often faster, harder, or more strongly than it would have on its own.

Think of it as giving a push — not a physical push, but a push of motivation or energy — that gets something moving or accelerates something already in motion. The key idea is that something acts as a trigger or fuel that drives a person, a process, or an event forward.

Imagine someone who has been sitting still, unsure whether to act. Then something happens — maybe they hear a powerful speech, maybe they face a challenge, maybe an opportunity appears — and suddenly they feel driven to move. That thing that pushed them into action? That thing spurred them.

The same logic applies to non-human things too — a company, an economy, a trend, a reaction — anything that gets a boost or gets triggered by an outside force.
The Two Main Ways "Spur" Is Used

1. To spur a person — meaning to motivate or drive them to do something

Here, spurring means pushing someone emotionally or mentally so that they feel the urge to act, try harder, or keep going.

"The teacher's encouraging words spurred the student to study even harder."

"Losing the match spurred him to train every single day."

"Her passion for justice spurred her to become a lawyer."

Notice: the person who is spurred doesn't just want to act — they feel genuinely driven, almost compelled. It's stronger than just "encouraged."

2. To spur a thing or process — meaning to cause or accelerate it

Here, spurring means acting as the trigger or catalyst that makes something start happening or happen more rapidly. This use is very common when talking about economies, growth, change, reactions, discussions, etc.

"The invention of the smartphone spurred massive changes in how people communicate."

"The drought spurred a nationwide debate about water conservation."

"The government's investment spurred economic growth in rural areas."

"His controversial speech spurred a wave of protests across the country."

Notice: in these cases, "spur" tells you what caused or accelerated something. It's not just that the thing happened — something specific pushed it into motion or sped it up.
The Grammar: How to Build Sentences With "Spur"

Pattern 1: spur + someone/something

"The crisis spurred action."
"Her words spurred him."

Pattern 2: spur + someone + to + verb

"The challenge spurred her to work harder."
"The news spurred them to reconsider their plan."

Pattern 3: spur + someone/something + into + noun

"The accident spurred the government into action."
"The bad reviews spurred the team into making major changes."

Pattern 4: spur + someone/something + on (phrasal verb — very common)

"The cheering crowd spurred the runners on."
"Despite the setbacks, her belief in herself spurred her on."

"Spur on" means to keep someone going — to encourage them to continue with energy and determination, especially when things are difficult.

This is where many learners miss the depth of the word. "Spur" is not a gentle or neutral word. It carries a sense of urgency, energy, and momentum. When something spurs you, it doesn't just politely invite you to act — it ignites something in you. Similarly, when something spurs a process, it doesn't just gradually nudge it along — it gives it a real push.

Compare these:

  • "The report mentioned the need for change." (neutral, passive)
  • "The report spurred immediate change." (active, energetic — something actually happened as a result)

Spur implies a cause-and-effect relationship where the result is real and often significant.
The Strength of "Spur" Compared to Similar Words

WordWhat it implies

"Encourage" is softer. You can encourage someone and they may or may not act. "Spur" implies they actually got moving.

"Cause" is more neutral and mechanical. "Spur" carries the added sense of driving force and energy — it sounds more dynamic.

"Motivate" is about creating internal desire. "Spur" focuses more on the external trigger that produces action — often with a sense of urgency or speed.

"Trigger" is close to "spur" but more abrupt and sudden. "Spur" can be more sustained — you can spur someone on over a period of time.

These are words you'll very often see next to "spur" in real usage:

  • Spur growth — "Low interest rates spurred economic growth."
  • Spur innovation — "Competition among companies spurs innovation."
  • Spur debate — "The new policy spurred fierce debate."
  • Spur action — "The shocking images spurred the public into action."
  • Spur demand — "The sale spurred demand for their products."
  • Spur development — "Investment in infrastructure spurred regional development."
  • Spur someone on — "His teammates spurred him on during the final lap."
  • Spur change — "The pandemic spurred rapid changes in healthcare."

1. "Spur" always needs a clear cause and a clear effect.
Something (person, event, idea, emotion) does the spurring, and something else (a person's action, a process, a change) gets spurred. If you use "spur," make sure both the driving force and the result are clear.

✅ "His anger spurred him to speak up."
❌ "He was spurred." (too vague — spurred by what? to do what?)

2. "Spur" often implies the result actually happened (or is likely to happen).
Unlike "try to motivate," when you say something spurred a result, you're usually saying the result actually occurred.

"The funding spurred research." → Research actually happened.

3. "Spur" is usually used in formal or semi-formal writing and speech.
It's perfectly natural in everyday English, but you'll see it especially in news articles, academic writing, and serious conversations. You would comfortably use it in an essay, a professional email, or a news report.
A Few Rich, Varied Examples to Cement the Word

"A single conversation with her mentor spurred her to quit her job and start her own business."

"The outbreak spurred scientists around the world to collaborate on a vaccine."

"Nothing spurs creativity quite like a tight deadline."

"Failures early in life spurred him on rather than breaking him down."

"The team's early success spurred investors to pour in more money."

"It was her daughter's diagnosis that finally spurred her into action."

To spur = to push, drive, or cause someone or something to act, move faster, or develop — by providing a strong motivating force or trigger.

If you remember just one thing: "spur" = a push that makes something go.
14056:
Something spurious looks real, genuine, or valid on the surface — but is actually false, fake, or flawed underneath. The word carries a specific and important idea: the appearance of being legitimate. A spurious thing isn't just wrong — it pretends to be right.

Think of it this way: a counterfeit banknote is spurious. It looks exactly like real money. It's designed to pass as real. But it isn't. That gap between looking real and being real is the heart of "spurious."

You might wonder: why not just say "false" or "fake"? Because those words don't carry the same weight.

  • False simply means not true.
  • Fake means not real.
  • Spurious means deceptively appearing to be true or real.

The deceptive appearance is baked into the word. When you call something spurious, you're saying: "This thing is passing itself off as something it's not."

1. Arguments and reasoning
This is one of the most common uses. A spurious argument sounds logical and well-constructed, but contains a hidden flaw or is built on a false foundation. It can fool people who don't look closely.

Example: "The politician made a spurious argument that crime had fallen because of his new policy, ignoring that crime rates had been declining for a decade before he took office."

2. Correlations and data (especially in science)
A spurious correlation is when two things appear to be connected in data, but the connection is accidental or meaningless — there's no real relationship between them.

A famous example: data shows that as ice cream sales rise, drowning rates also rise. They track together perfectly. But ice cream doesn't cause drowning — both simply increase in summer when it's hot and people swim more. That's a spurious correlation. The apparent link is real in the numbers but completely meaningless in reality.

3. Documents and objects
A spurious document is a forged or fabricated one — something designed to look official or authentic when it isn't.

Example: "The historian discovered that the letter, long believed to be written by Napoleon, was spurious — it had been forged in the 1900s."

4. Emotions and behavior
Feelings or gestures can be spurious too — performed or faked, designed to look genuine.

Example: "He expressed spurious concern for the workers while privately cutting their wages."

5. Claims and evidence
In everyday language, a spurious claim is one that lacks real support but is packaged to sound credible.

Example: "The advertisement made spurious claims about the product curing disease, with no scientific evidence."

Here's an important nuance: something can be spurious without intentional deception. In science, for instance, a spurious result can emerge from flawed methodology — the researcher wasn't lying, but the result still doesn't reflect reality. However, spurious can also imply deliberate fraud, depending on context. The word itself doesn't specify — context tells you which is happening.

These words are close to spurious, but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Specious — Very similar, but almost exclusively used for arguments and reasoning. A specious argument is one that seems valid and even clever, but is fundamentally flawed. Spurious is broader — it applies to documents, emotions, data, and more.
  • Bogus — Informal. Means false or fake, but lacks the formal weight of spurious.
  • Counterfeit — Specifically about objects (money, signatures, goods) made to look real.
  • Fraudulent — Emphasizes intentional deception for personal gain.
  • Fabricated — Made up entirely.
  • Sham — A complete fake; often refers to situations or relationships.
The opposites of spurious are: genuine, authentic, legitimate, valid, real, bona fide.

"Spurious" is a formal word. You'll see it in academic papers, scientific writing, journalism, legal language, and serious essays. It's rarely used in casual conversation — saying "that's a spurious excuse" in everyday talk sounds sophisticated and deliberate. Using it signals precision and careful thought.
A Simple Test to Remember It

Whenever you're unsure if something fits the word "spurious," ask yourself:

Does this thing wear the costume of truth or legitimacy, but hide a false or hollow reality underneath?

If yes — that's spurious.
Spurious describes something that appears genuine, valid, or real but is actually false, flawed, or fake — with the emphasis always on that misleading surface appearance.
14057:
To spurn someone or something means to reject it with contempt or scorn — not just to say "no," but to push it away with a sense of pride, disgust, or disdain. When you spurn something, you are making it clear that you consider it beneath you, unworthy of you, or deeply unwanted.

Think of it as a rejection that carries an extra emotional sting. It's the difference between politely declining a gift and throwing it back in someone's face.

Many words describe rejection — refuse, decline, reject, dismiss. But spurn is different in one important way: it always carries an attitude. There is pride, contempt, or scorn baked into it. When someone spurns something, they are not just saying "no thank you." They are saying "no, and I want nothing to do with this."

This is why spurn is often used in emotional, high-stakes situations — unrequited love, rejected peace offerings, dismissed advice from someone who cared. The word feels sharp and final. It conveys that the person doing the spurning had a strong, dismissive reaction — not a casual or reluctant one.

Spurn always has two roles: the person doing the rejecting, and the person (or thing) being rejected.

The person being spurned is usually someone who offered something sincerely — love, help, a proposal, advice, loyalty. The person doing the spurning pushes that offer away, often coldly or proudly. This is why being spurned hurts more than being simply rejected. It feels like a deliberate, contemptuous dismissal.

You can spurn a person, an offer, an idea, or an opportunity.

These will help you see how the word moves and feels in real use:

  • She spurned his romantic advances and walked away without a word. — She rejected him coldly and dismissively.
  • The proud king spurned the enemy's offer of peace, calling it an insult. — He rejected it with contempt.
  • He had worked hard to earn her trust, but she spurned every attempt he made. — She pushed away his efforts with disdain.
  • The young artist spurned his mentor's advice, convinced he knew better. — He dismissively brushed off the guidance.
  • They spurned the chance to settle the dispute peacefully, choosing conflict instead. — They rejected the opportunity with scorn or stubborn pride.

Notice how in every case, the rejection feels charged — it's never neutral or polite.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as understanding what it does.

Spurn ≠ Decline. Declining is polite and gentle. "I'm afraid I must decline your invitation." There's no contempt there.

Spurn ≠ Refuse. Refusing is firm, but not necessarily emotional. "He refused to sign the contract." Clean, neutral.

Spurn ≠ Ignore. Ignoring means paying no attention. Spurning is an active rejection — you acknowledge the offer and push it away with attitude.

Spurn ≠ Reject (in casual use). "Reject" is a general, all-purpose word. "Spurn" is sharper, more emotional, and almost always implies that the thing being rejected deserved better treatment than it received.
The Emotional Texture of the Word

"Spurn" tends to appear in situations where the stakes are emotional. You'll find it in literature, formal writing, and serious speech more than in everyday casual conversation. If someone says "she spurned him," it paints a vivid picture — the cold shoulder, the wounded party, the proud dismisser.

The word also carries a slight moral undertone. Often, the reader or listener feels sympathy for the one who was spurned, because being spurned implies that something worthy — love, goodwill, an honest offer — was treated with undeserved contempt.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

To spurn = to reject something with contempt or scorn, making it clear you find it unworthy or beneath you.

If you remember that single idea — rejection wrapped in contempt — you will never misuse or misunderstand this word.
14058: "Spurt" has two closely related meanings. Both share the same core idea: something happening suddenly, briefly, and with noticeable force or intensity. Once you grasp that core idea, both meanings feel natural.
Meaning 1: A sudden, forceful short stream of liquid

A spurt of liquid is when a liquid shoots out suddenly, in a short burst, with some force — not a slow drip, and not a long steady flow, but a quick, forceful gush.

Examples:

  • When you squeeze a lemon too hard, a spurt of juice flies out.
  • If a pipe cracks under pressure, water comes out in spurts.
  • A small cut on your finger might release a spurt of blood when you press it.

What makes it a "spurt" and not just any flow of liquid?
Three things define it: it's sudden, it's brief, and it has force behind it. A gentle, slow trickle is not a spurt. A long, steady stream is not a spurt. A spurt is that quick, shooting burst — almost like the liquid is being pushed or squeezed out.

You'll often see it in the phrase "in spurts", meaning the liquid isn't flowing continuously but shooting out in short repeated bursts. For example: "The old tap released water in spurts before finally stopping."
Meaning 2: A sudden, short burst of increased activity, speed, or effort

This is the more widely used meaning in everyday life. Here, "spurt" doesn't refer to liquid at all — it refers to a brief period of doing something much more intensely or quickly than usual.

Think of it this way: imagine someone walking at a relaxed pace, then suddenly running fast for 30 seconds, then going back to walking. That 30 seconds of running is a spurt of speed.

Examples:

  • "She had a spurt of energy after her nap and cleaned the whole kitchen."
  • "The team worked slowly all week but had a final spurt of productivity before the deadline."
  • "He ran at a steady pace but put on a sudden spurt near the finish line to overtake his rival."

The key qualities are exactly the same as in Meaning 1 — sudden, brief, and noticeably intense. It's not gradual and it doesn't last long. It stands out from what came before and after it.

You will almost certainly encounter the phrase growth spurt — it's extremely common. A growth spurt is when a child (or sometimes an animal or plant) grows noticeably faster than usual over a short period. A child might seem the same height for months, and then suddenly grow several centimetres in just a few weeks. That sudden, brief, intense period of growth is called a growth spurt.

It's also used more broadly:

  • "The company experienced a growth spurt after launching its new product." (It grew rapidly for a short time.)
How "spurt" feels compared to similar words

• Compared to trickle: A trickle is slow and gentle. A spurt is fast and forceful. They are opposites in feel.
  • Compared to stream or flow: A stream or flow is continuous and steady. A spurt is short and sudden.
  • Compared to surge: A surge can be large and sustained (like a surge of electricity or a tidal surge). A spurt is always brief and smaller in scale. A spurt of energy fades quickly; a surge of energy is bigger and lasts longer.
  • Compared to burst: Very close in feel. But "burst" often implies something breaking open (a balloon bursts, a pipe bursts). A "spurt" focuses specifically on what comes out — the stream of liquid or the brief moment of intense activity.
How to know you're using it correctly

Ask yourself two questions:

  1. Is it sudden (not gradual)?
  2. Is it brief (not sustained)?

If yes to both, "spurt" fits. A long period of hard work is not a spurt — it would be a stretch, a stint, or a run. But a sudden 20-minute burst of hard work in an otherwise quiet day? That's a spurt.

A spurt is something that happens suddenly and briefly, with noticeable intensity — either a forceful short stream of liquid shooting out, or a short period of heightened speed, energy, growth, or effort. The word always carries that feeling of sudden + brief + intense. Those three qualities are the soul of the word.
14059:
When something spurts, it shoots out suddenly, with force, in a quick, pressured stream. Think of pressing your thumb against a garden hose — the water doesn't just flow out gently; it shoots out in a fast, forceful burst. That's spurting.

The word carries three key qualities at once: suddenness, pressure/force, and briefness. Something that spurts doesn't trickle slowly, and it doesn't pour steadily for a long time — it bursts out in a quick, energetic rush.

Sense 1 — A liquid (or substance) shoots out suddenly

This is the most common use. When a liquid spurts, it is ejected or released with force, usually from a small opening, under pressure.

  • When he cut his finger deeply, blood spurted from the wound.
  • She squeezed the ketchup bottle too hard and it spurted all over the table.
  • The cracked pipe spurted water across the basement floor.
  • He bit into the ripe tomato and juice spurted down his chin.

Notice in all these cases: the liquid isn't calmly dripping or gently flowing — it's shooting out with some force, quickly, in a stream.

This sense can work in two ways grammatically:

  • The liquid itself spurts: Blood spurted from the cut. (The blood is doing the spurting.)
  • Something causes liquid to spurt: The hose spurted water everywhere. (The hose is causing the water to shoot out.)

Both are perfectly natural.

Sense 2 — A person, animal, or vehicle suddenly moves fast for a short time

Here, "spurt" describes a sudden short burst of speed or acceleration — moving ahead quickly for a brief moment, usually in the context of a race, competition, or chase.

  • In the final stretch of the race, she spurted ahead and crossed the finish line first.
  • The rabbit spurted forward the moment it sensed the fox approaching.
  • The car spurted past us and disappeared around the corner.
  • He had been jogging at a steady pace, but spurted when he saw the finish line.

The key here is that the movement is sudden and temporary — a short, sharp burst, not a sustained, long-distance sprint. After a spurt of speed, a person might slow back down.
What Makes "Spurt" Different From Similar Words

Since "spurt" lives in a neighbourhood of words that all describe liquid or fast movement, it's important to know exactly where it sits among them.

Spurt vs. drip: When something drips, it falls in slow, separate drops — no force, no speed, no stream. Spurting is the opposite energy entirely.

Spurt vs. flow: Flow is smooth, steady, and continuous — like a river flowing. Spurting is abrupt and pressured, not calm or continuous.

Spurt vs. gush: Gush involves a large, dramatic rush of liquid — a big volume pouring out rapidly. Spurting is more focused and narrower. A burst pipe might gush water; a punctured vein spurts blood. Gushing tends to be more generous in volume; spurting is sharper and more jet-like.

Spurt vs. squirt: These two are very close, and in everyday use people often use them interchangeably. However, squirt usually emphasises a thin, directed, intentional stream (you squirt a water gun at someone deliberately). Spurt more often implies something happening suddenly, sometimes with less control, under pressure — it can feel more accidental or forceful. Blood spurts; you squirt lemon juice onto fish.

Spurt vs. spray: Spray scatters liquid in many directions at once — like a sprinkler or a sneeze. Spurting is a single stream, not a scattered mist.

"Spurt" has a slightly visceral, physical feel to it. It often appears in contexts involving the body (blood, sweat, saliva, juice), machines under pressure (pipes, hoses, engines), and athletic competition (running, racing). It's not a gentle or elegant word — it suggests rawness, pressure, and a lack of complete control. Things that spurt often do so because something built up and then released, or because something was squeezed or broken.

Less commonly, "spurt" can describe a sudden brief increase in something abstract — activity, growth, or interest — that mirrors the idea of a short burst of energy.

  • The economy spurted briefly after the tax cuts, then slowed again.
  • His motivation spurted at the start of the project but faded quickly.

This usage is much less frequent than the physical senses, but you may encounter it.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To spurt is to shoot out suddenly and forcefully in a stream (liquid) or to move suddenly fast for a short time (speed). The word always implies something brief, pressured, and abrupt — never slow, gentle, or sustained.
